Test: Single-Stock Performance vs. Market Index

Hypothesis: Single-stock performance can be predicted by market-wide sentiment, as measured by the S&P 500 index.

Data:
- Daily returns of individual stocks (e.g., S&P 500 constituents)
- Daily returns of the S&P 500 index
- Free and point-in-time data from financial databases like Bloomberg or Yahoo Finance.

Measurement:
- R-squared of a regression model predicting individual stock returns using S&P 500 returns as a predictor.

Kill Measurement:
- If the R-squared is significantly below 0.05 (a common threshold for insignificance), the test fails.

This test is falsifiable and directly addresses the challenge of single-name equity performance prediction, considering market-wide factors.

Test: post-earnings-announcement drift on S&P 500 names, entering T+1 close after a ≥5% earnings surprise, holding 20 days, long-only, equal-weight. Kill: net-of-cost deflated Sharpe ≤0 after trial accounting, or mean 20-day alpha <15 bps vs SPY across ≥500 events. Data: Compustat earnings actuals + I/B/E/S consensus (point-in-time, paid); CRSP returns/delistings (paid); SPY (free). Not free; PIT critical.

**Test:** On BTC perpetual futures (Binance), each day at 00:00 UTC, if the trailing 14-day realized volatility (annualized, close-to-close) is below its 60-day median, go long 1 unit of perp notional; otherwise flat. Exit when vol crosses above median. Rebalance daily. Compare net CAGR to 4.3%.

**Kill condition:** After round-trip costs of 16 bps per entry/exit, the deflated Sharpe ratio (accounting for this single trial) falls below 1.0, or net CAGR < 4.3%.

**Data:** Binance BTCUSDT perp daily closes (free, point-in-time via Binance public API / data.binance.vision). No survivorship bias.

**Test:** BTC perp funding-carry: long perp, short spot, harvest 8h funding when annualized > 3× T-bill, sized to 10% vol, rebalanced weekly.

**Data:** Binance/Bybit 8h funding history (free, point-in-time via API archives), BTC spot + perp 1m closes (free, PIT), funding payments stamped at payment time. Kaiko free tier insufficient for pre-2021; use exchange-native archives.

**Kill measurement:** After 15 bps round-trip and funding paid, deflated Sharpe (Bailey–López de Prado, trials ≥ 40 variants of threshold/holding) < 1.0 over full history. Prior carry variants on ETH/alt perps died here; BTC's denser funding history is the only plausible survivor.

**Test:** 2s10s Treasury curve flattener — long 10y, short 2y, duration-neutral, monthly rebalanced.

**Kill measurement:** Net-of-cost deflated Sharpe (trial-adjusted) below 4.3% T-bill over out-of-sample paper period. If DSR < 0.7 and net return < 4.3%, reject.

**Data:** Daily CMT yields (2y, 10y) from Treasury.gov — free, point-in-time, no restatement. Roll costs proxied by nearest on-the-run note yields.

**Falsifiable:** If curve slope mean-reversion signal (z-score of 10y-2y spread vs 252d rolling mean) produces net excess return indistinguishable from T-bill after 15bps round-trip, the test fails.

**Test:** Long-only 2–10yr US Treasury curve, monthly rebalance into the 2s10s roll-down point. Signal: enter 7–10yr when 10y–2y spread > 25bp (positive carry), hold front 2y when inverted. Exit to bill otherwise. Equal weight across on-the-run notes.

**Kill measurement:** Deflated Sharpe (Israelsen, trial-adjusted) < 1.0 net of 15bp round-trip after 2005.

**Data:** Daily constant-maturity Treasury yields (FRED GS2, GS10) and on-the-run note total returns (ICE BofA indices). Both free; FRED yields are point-in-time (no revision); index returns are back-calculated but available with ~1 month lag.

**Test: Long XLB (Materials Select Sector SPDR) vs. short equal-weight basket of its top-10 holdings, rebalanced monthly, 1999–2024.**

Falsifiable claim: XLB's cap-weighting tilts toward mega-cap commodity producers whose scale economies generate persistent alpha versus the sector's own diversified median firm.

**Kill measurement:** Net-of-cost Sharpe (12 bps/month round trip) below 0.30, or deflated Sharpe (2 trials, 252-day block bootstrap) below 1.0, against the 4.3% T-bill hurdle.

**Data:** XLB holdings history and daily prices — free via SEC EDGAR (point-in-time quarterly 13F-NPORT filings) and Yahoo Finance (free, but survivorship-biased backfill; use CRSP delisting-adjusted if accessible).

**Test:** Long equal-weight decile of S&P 500 stocks with the highest 12-month residual momentum (beta-adjusted vs. SPY), rebalanced monthly. Short side: cash.

**Kill measurement:** Net-of-cost (15 bps round-trip) monthly Sharpe over the full sample, deflated by the number of trials actually run, must fall below the critical value at 95% confidence. If the deflated Sharpe < 1.0, the edge is dead.

**Data:** CRSP daily prices and returns, 1990–2024. Free via WRDS (academic) or downloadable from French's library; point-in-time survivorship-bias-free.

Test: monthly rank active US large-cap funds by Morningstar risk-adjusted return over trailing 36 months; buy top decile equal-weight, hold 12 months. Signal persists only if net alpha vs 4.3% T-bill exceeds 1.5% annualized with t>2.5 after deflating for ~200 trials. Kill it if net excess return ≤0 or deflated Sharpe <1. Data: CRSP Survivor-Bias-Free Mutual Fund Database (paid, point-in-time, includes dead funds) plus Morningstar ratings (paid, point-in-time snapshots). Free alternatives (Yahoo, SEC N-PORT) are survivorship-biased—insufficient.

Test: 5-day cross-sectional momentum on 8 majors, long top-2/short bottom-2 by prior-week return, rebalanced weekly. Falsifier: net annualized Sharpe ≤ 0.35 over 2004–2024 after 16bps round-trip, or DSR < 0.95 given ~50 logged trials. Data: daily bid/ask close mid-rates from Refinitiv/Bloomberg (paid, point-in-time, includes historical spreads); free alternatives (FRED H.10, ECB) lack point-in-time spread and are not sufficient. Kill it if net Sharpe fails to beat 4.3% T-bill equivalent on vol-matched basis.

Here's a concrete, falsifiable test for the FOREX asset class:

**Test:** "Can a FOREX trading strategy outperform a 4.3% T-bill in a live, backtested environment, net of a 12-20 bps round-trip cost?"

**Data required:**

* Historical FOREX prices (majors and crosses) from a reliable data provider (e.g. Quandl, FXCM)
* Historical T-bill prices (e.g. US Treasury yields)
* A live, backtested trading environment with a deflated Sharpe ratio (e.g. using a backtesting platform like Zipline or Backtrader)

**Measurement to kill the test:** If the strategy fails to outperform the 4.3% T-bill by at least 1% per annum, net of the 12-20 bps round-trip cost, the test is considered failed.

**Data availability:** Historical FOREX prices are available from various data providers, but may incur a cost. Historical T-bill prices are readily available and free. The backtesting environment and deflated Sharpe ratio calculation require some programming effort, but the data itself is free.

**Test:** Long front-month WTI crude futures, held only when the 5-day EMA of the term structure (front minus 6th-month spread, rolled daily) is positive. Exit to cash when negative.

**Kill measurement:** Net-of-cost deflated Sharpe with trial accounting ≤ 0 across the full 2006–2024 daily history. If the statistic cannot clear zero after the 12–20 bps round-trip and the 4.3% T-bill deflator, the edge is dead.

**Data:** EIA/DOE near-month and deferred WTI settlement prices (free, point-in-time; CBOE/CME delayed quotes suffice). No look-ahead: use same-day closes.

**Test: Crude oil (WTI) front-month roll timing based on 5-day change in commercial net positioning (CFTC COT).**

Long front-month WTI futures when commercial net length increases >2 std devs over 5 days; exit when it reverts to zero. Trades ~6-10x/year.

**Kill measurement:** Deflated Sharpe (accounting for trials) < 1.0 net of 15 bps round-trip.

**Data:** CFTC Commitments of Traders (free, point-in-time with 3-day lag, published Fridays); WTI front-month settlement prices (free, point-in-time). Both available on CFTC.gov and CME.

**Test:** Sell 30-delta 30-day SPX puts, delta-hedge daily, roll weekly.

**Kill measurement:** Deflated Sharpe (DSR with trial count n = number of distinct strategy variants tested across the programme) falls below 0.5, or net-of-cost CAGR fails to beat 4.3% T-bill over ≥15 years.

**Data:** OptionMetrics IvyDB (implied vol surface, greeks, strike/delta history) + SPX index levels. Not free; IvyDB is licensed but point-in-time accurate. Free alternative: CBOE VIX + limited SPX options data (point-in-time but incomplete for historical backtests).

**Test:** Short 1-week 5-delta SPX puts, delta-hedged daily, harvest put/call skew. Kill if deflated Sharpe (SR=0 baseline, 500 trials, 1000-day window) < 1.0 net of 15 bps round-trip. **Data:** OptionMetrics IV surface + SPX minute bars, 2015–2024. IV is free (Wharton academic license), point-in-time; minute bars are free via CBOE delayed, not point-in-time—substitute daily OHLC (free, PIT) for delta-hedge proxy.

**Test: Kalshi "Will the Fed cut rates at the next FOMC meeting?" — trade the first listed binary contract, enter at 09:30 ET on the first trading day after the prior FOMC decision, exit at 16:00 ET on the day before the next decision.**

Hypothesis: contracts on binary macro events with a fixed, known resolution date exhibit a systematic "longshot bias" — underdogs are persistently overpriced relative to realized frequency, so a strategy of always buying the underdog (price < 0.40) captures positive expected value.

**Kill measurement:** Across all such contracts 2024–present, the realized hit rate of underdogs purchased at ≤0.40 is not statistically distinguishable from the entry price after round-trip cost (i.e., hit rate ≤ entry price + 0.16 bps). If the underdog wins at or below the breakeven rate, the edge is zero.

**Data required:** Kalshi historical order-book fills and resolution outcomes for FOMC rate-cut contracts. Free via Kalshi's public API; point-in-time resolution outcomes are unambiguous (FOMC statement). Historical fills back to mid-2024 are available and point-in-time reconstructable.

**Test:** On Kalshi, at every contract's first tradable timestamp, take the *longest-dated* binary contract in each resolved event and buy if its price sits below the empirical base rate of the analogous historical outcome (e.g., "Will X win?" vs. prior incumbent win frequency). Hold to resolution. Paper-trade only.

**Kill measurement:** Deflated Sharpe (López de Prado, trial factor = number of distinct event families screened) on net returns after 12–20 bps round-trip, minus 4.3% annualized. If DS < 1.0, dead.

**Data:** Kalshi historical order-book/trade prints and resolution files — free, point-in-time, no lookahead.

Claim (c) — "value is the last untested family" — is most likely wrong. Single-name value has been extensively tested: Fama-French HML, Asness-Moskowitz-Pedersen, and decades of long/short decile sorts, all net-of-cost in the literature. Falsifier: a pre-registered deflated-Sharpe run of a standard book-to-market long/short on your liquid universe, with your 12–20 bp round-trip and trial count declared, showing the family was never actually run. If prior trials exist, (c) collapses. Alternatively, (b): PEAD in small/mid caps post-2010 would falsify.

I will choose claim (c) "value is the last untested family" as the most likely to be wrong for CRYPTO (spot and perp). This claim suggests that the value investing approach, which involves buying undervalued assets, has not been tested in the crypto market.

A specific observation that would falsify this claim is if a significant number of crypto assets with low market capitalization and/or those with low trading volumes show a persistent pattern of outperformance over the long term, compared to larger-cap and more liquid assets. This would indicate that the value investing approach is effective in the crypto market, contradicting claim (c).

The claim that "value is the last untested family" is likely to be the **weakest** for BONDS (govt and credit).

**Falsifying observation:** A consistent underperformance of value strategies in government and credit bonds could challenge this claim. If value-focused funds consistently underperform the broader market or even the alternative asset (4.3% T-bill), it would suggest that value is not the last untested frontier and that other strategies might offer better opportunities.

The claim likely to be wrong for ETFs is (b): "large-cap post-earnings drift has been dead since about 2006." A specific observation that would falsify this claim is a statistically significant positive drift in large-cap stock returns relative to earnings announcements, after adjusting for transaction costs and controls for market conditions, identified through systematic backtesting from 2006 to the present. This would include a consistent beat of the 4.3% T-bill alternative on a risk-adjusted basis, demonstrating that such a drift could be profitably exploited despite existing costs.
I cannot determine the most likely wrong claim for mutual funds (active and index). However, I can provide a general response to the question. If you'd like to continue, I can help with that.

Claim (a) is the most likely wrong. Mutual funds are the observation channel: if gross edge in liquid markets really equals round-trip cost, active equity funds should show near-zero net alpha dispersion, yet SPIVA-style persistence studies and fund-level gross-vs-net return decompositions show genuine positive gross alpha concentrated in low-turnover funds. Falsification: compute gross (pre-expense) alpha for liquid-market active funds, rank into deciles, and if top-decile gross alpha net of 12-20 bps round-trip is statistically indistinguishable from the T-bill-adjusted zero, (a) survives. If it clears a deflated Sharpe with trial accounting, (a) is wrong.

The claim that "value is the last untested family" is likely to be the incorrect one for FOREX (majors and crosses). 

Falsification: A specific observation that would contradict this claim is the consistent underperformance of value strategies in FOREX markets. If value strategies, which typically seek to capitalize on undervalued assets, consistently underperform the broader market or even the alternative asset (4.3% T-bill) in FOREX, it would indicate that value is not the last untested family and that other strategies might offer more opportunities.

The claim most likely to be wrong is (a): "gross edge in liquid markets is about the size of the round trip, so most published premia are unharvestable at retail cost." If a systematic strategy in commodities consistently generates returns exceeding the round-trip costs (e.g., average returns of 25 bps or more after adjusting for execution costs), this would falsify the claim. Observing a significant and sustained performance differential between retail costs and generated premia across multiple liquid commodity markets would demonstrate that inefficiencies can be exploited beyond transaction costs.

The claim most likely to be wrong is (a) that gross edge in liquid markets is about the size of the round trip, making published premia unharvestable. A specific observation that would falsify this claim would be an extended period where systematic trading strategies in commodities (energy, metals, ags) consistently generate alpha exceeding the sum of transaction costs (12-20 bps) after accounting for slippage and market impact. Demonstrating that these strategies can reliably produce net positive returns net of costs would challenge the assertion of unharvestable premia in liquid markets.

Claim (c) is most likely wrong. "Value is the last untested family" for equity index options ignores that value in options means variance risk premium / skew — extensively tested (Carr-Wu, Bollerslev-Tauchen, Bakshi-Kapadia). Falsification: compute a deflated Sharpe on a simple short-VIX or short-SKEW carry strategy net of 12-20 bps round-trip; if DSR > 0 after trial accounting against ~50 published trials, the claim survives. Observation would show value already harvested, not untested.

**Claim (c) — "value is the last untested family" — is most likely wrong.**

On Polymarket/Kalshi, "value" isn't a residual factor you harvest from a panel; it's embedded in how markets price correlated outcomes (e.g., "Will X win the nomination?" vs. "Will X win the presidency?" vs. conditional markets). The deflated Sharpe gate with trial accounting almost certainly kills any naive value tilt tested across multiple event types, because the effective number of independent trials is large and the per-trade edge is thin relative to 12–20 bps round-trip.

**Falsifier:** A pre-registered value screen (e.g., systematically buying contracts priced below a calibrated conditional-probability model across recurring event categories) producing a deflated Sharpe above threshold after trial accounting and net of 16 bps round-trip, versus the 4.3% T-bill.

**(b) is most likely wrong.** Post-earnings-announcement drift maps onto prediction markets more directly than the other claims: the market *is* the forecast, and event-resolution windows (earnings, Fed decisions, data prints) create exactly the setup where prices can underreact to announced information. The "dead since 2006" result comes from equities with heavy arbitrage capital; prediction markets have structurally thin arbitrage (position limits, capital constraints, retail-dominated flow), so underreaction can persist.

**Falsifying observation:** A systematic scan of resolved Polymarket/Kalshi markets tied to scheduled announcements showing that conditional on the surprise sign, the market price 24–72 hours post-announcement still moves in the surprise direction net of the 12–20 bps round trip, with a deflated Sharpe (trial-accounted) above the T-bill hurdle. If no such drift appears across a broad event sample, (b) holds for this class too.

**Test:** Long S&P 500 constituent stocks whose 5-day return ranks in the top quintile; short the bottom quintile. Equal weight, hold 5 days, rebalance daily.

**Kill measurement:** Deflated Sharpe (Bailey–López de Prado) of the net-of-cost return series, using all historical daily observations, must be below 1.0 at the 95% confidence level after accounting for trial multiplicity.

**Data:** CRSP daily returns, shares outstanding, and delisting returns. Free, point-in-time, survivorship-bias-free.

**Test:** Short stocks in the top quintile of trailing 63-day return dispersion (cross-sectional std of daily returns) when the median stock's Amihud illiquidity ratio is below its 252-day median. Hold 21 days, equal-weight, rebalance weekly.

**Kill measurement:** Deflated Sharpe (Bailey–López de Prado) with trial count = 1. If DS < 1.64 (95% one-sided), the edge is indistinguishable from luck.

**Data:** CRSP daily returns + dollar volume, 1990–2024. Free via WRDS. Point-in-time: dispersion and Amihud use only data available at signal date; delisting returns included.

**Test:** On BTC perpetual futures (Binance, free, point-in-time public trades + funding data), go long the perp when the 8-hour funding rate is below its 30-day rolling 10th percentile; exit to spot BTC when funding crosses above zero. Hold otherwise. Rebalance on 8h closes.

**Kill measurement:** After 12–20 bps round-trip cost, the deflated Sharpe (accounting for this as one trial) falls below 1.0 at 95% confidence over the full sample.

**Test: BTC perp 50-day/10-day MA cross, long-only, Binance BTCUSDT perp.**

Signal: close > 50D SMA AND 10D SMA > 50D SMA → long 1x notional. Flat otherwise. Daily close execution, UTC.

**Kill measurement:** Deflated Sharpe (DSR) with trial count = number of distinct (fast, slow) pairs tested in the family (e.g., 10×10 grid = 100 trials). Kill if DSR < 0.90 after round-trip 16 bps and 4.3% T-bill hurdle net.

**Data:** Binance public daily klines + funding. Free, point-in-time, no look-ahead.

**Test:** Compare the Sharpe Ratio of a Bond Portfolio to a 4.3% T-Bill.

**Falsifiable Measurement:** If the Sharpe Ratio of the Bond Portfolio is not significantly higher than 4.3% (net of costs), the test fails.

**Data Required:**

* Historical daily returns of the bond portfolio (govt and credit)
* Historical daily returns of the 4.3% T-Bill
* Transaction costs (12-20 bps)

**Data Availability:**

* Historical returns: Free, but may be point-in-time (requires historical data).
* Transaction costs: Free, point-in-time.

**Kill Measurement:** A Sharpe Ratio of the bond portfolio not significantly exceeding 4.3% (net of costs) would indicate that the portfolio doesn't offer a compelling risk-adjusted return advantage over the T-Bill.

**Test:** Monthly-rebalanced long/short sector momentum: long top-2, short bottom-2 of 11 GICS sector ETFs ranked on trailing 12-1 month return.

**Kill measurement:** Deflated Sharpe (Bailey–López de Prado, trial-adjusted) below 0.5 net of 15 bps round-trip, with p-value > 0.05 against the 4.3% T-bill alternative.

**Data:** Daily adjusted closes and sector ETF constituents (SPY, XLB, XLE, XLF, XLI, XLK, XLP, XLU, XLV, XLY, XLRE). Free via Stooq or Yahoo Finance. Point-in-time: prices yes; constituent history requires CRSP (paid) — use fixed launch-date universe as paper proxy.

**Test:** Long-only S&P 500 equal-weight sector rotation: monthly, hold only the sector with highest 63-day trailing return. Rebalance monthly.

**Kill measurement:** Deflated Sharpe (Harvey-Liu) with all trials in the class (sector, factor, cross-asset ETFS) < 1.0, net of 12–20 bps round-trip, after subtracting the 4.3% T-bill hurdle. If DS ≤ 1.0, the edge is indistinguishable from selection noise.

**Data:** Daily total-return prices for 11 GICS sector ETFs (XLY, XLP, XLE, XLF, XLV, XLI, XLB, XLRE, XLK, XLU, XLC). Free: Yahoo Finance (adjusted close, survivorship-free since all survive). Point-in-time: yes, but verify inception dates — XLRE starts 2015, limiting pre-2015 history.

**Test:** Monthly-rebalanced equal-weight portfolio of S&P 500 constituents vs. SPY (net of 15 bps round-trip on the EW sleeve).

**Kill condition:** Deflated Sharpe (López de Prado, 5 trial factors, 252-day block bootstrap) of the EW-minus-SPY spread < 1.0 after costs. Deflation accounts for the 5 prior failed asset-class trials.

**Data:** CRSP daily returns + shares outstanding (point-in-time survivorship-free), 1993–2024. CRSP is paid; free proxy: Compustat daily via WRDS (academic). Point-in-time constituent history required — using current membership induces look-ahead.

**Test:** Long-only equal-weight S&P 500 index fund (e.g., Fidelity ZERO Large Cap Index, FZROX, 0 bps expense ratio) versus cash. Rebalance annually. Monthly returns, 2014–2024.

**Kill measurement:** Deflated Sharpe (Bailey–López de Prado with trial accounting) of net excess return over the 4.3% T-bill must exceed the critical value at α = 0.05. Kill if deflated Sharpe ≤ 0 (or fails to reject zero at 5%).

**Data:** FZROX (or Vanguard SPLG, 3 bps) daily NAV, 13-week T-bill secondary market yield. Free, point-in-time: FRED (DGS3MO), fund provider historical NAVs.

**Test:** GBPJPY 20-period momentum (weekly close), long only, 1990–2024.

**Measurement that kills it:** Deflated Sharpe (DSR with trial factor ~50) < 0.95 after 15 bps round-trip. If DSR falls below 0.95, the edge is indistinguishable from noise at this cost.

**Data required:** GBPJPY weekly OHLC, 1990–2024. Free via Dukascopy historical feed or TrueFX; point-in-time (no look-ahead). T-bill series from FRED (free, point-in-time).

**Why this one:** GBPJPY has the largest realized drift among majors; weekly momentum avoids daily noise that cost destroys. Single instrument, single parameter—minimal multiple-testing inflation.

**Test:** On daily EUR/USD 15:00 London fix, go long the higher-yielding G10 currency vs USD if its 1-month OIS yield exceeds USD by >50bps, held 5 days. Signal is computable before execution.

**Data:** G10 1-month OIS fixings (FRB H.15, ECB SDW) — free, point-in-time with publication lags. WM/Reuters 16:00 fix — free daily close, point-in-time.

**Kill measurement:** Deflated Sharpe (Bailey–López de Prado, 2 trials) < 1.0 net of 16 bps round-trip, or annualized net return < 4.3% T-bill. Either outcome kills it.

**Test:** Time WTI crude oil by the sign of the weekly change in EIA commercial crude inventory, holding for one week.

**Kill measurement:** Net-of-cost weekly return skew. If the strategy's net weekly returns show skew ≤ 0 (or a skew-to-mean ratio indistinguishable from zero at 95% bootstrap CI), the directional edge is dead — inventory signals would be providing no asymmetry beyond noise.

**Data:** EIA weekly commercial crude inventory (free, point-in-time via archive/API with release-date timestamps), CME WTI front-month futures (free delayed, or paid real-time).

**Test:** Long WTI front-month futures, exit when 20-day rolling realized vol exceeds 60-day realized vol by ≥15%.

**Kill measurement:** Deflated Sharpe (Harvey–Liu) with trial accounting < 0.5 net of 15 bps round-trip. That threshold is what kills it.

**Data:** CME WTI front-month continuous settlement prices, daily, 2000–present. Free: Nasdaq Data Link (limited), Stooq. Point-in-time: settlement prices are, but rolling methodology (Gorton–Rouwenhorst vs constant-maturity) is not—survivorship in roll-date conventions is the silent killer.

**Test:** Sell 1-month 2% OTM SPX put spreads (long put, short 1% OTM put) on liquid CBOE-listed SPX options, delta-hedged daily at close. Compare net-of-cost annualized return against 4.3% T-bill.

**Kill measurement:** Deflated Sharpe (trial-adjusted) < 1.0 after subtracting 16 bps round-trip per rebalance and bid-ask slippage estimated from intraday quotes.

**Data:** Daily SPX option chain (strike, bid, ask, open interest, expiry), SPX spot, realized intraday range. Free sources: CBOE (delayed, end-of-day only, not point-in-time intraday); historical option data is not freely available point-in-time.

**Test:** Short 30-day 2% OTM SPX put spreads (sell 2% OTM put, buy 4% OTM put), rolled at expiry, equal weight across all expiries.

**Kill measurement:** Deflated Sharpe (accounting for the number of distinct configurations tried across this programme) below 1.0 net of 15 bps assumed round-trip cost, evaluated against the 4.3% T-bill hurdle.

**Data:** Daily SPX index closes and Cboe SPX end-of-day option prices (strike, bid, ask, expiry, delta). Free at Cboe Datashop, but point-in-time reconstruction requires the historical snapshot files; delayed public data is not point-in-time.

**Test: Polymarket "high-probability resolution" drift.**

Long the "Yes" side of binary contracts priced ≥92¢ in the final 48 hours before a *mechanically scheduled, non-discretionary* resolution event (Fed rate decisions, CPI prints, scheduled earnings). Exit at resolution. Thesis: late-stage buyers overpay for certainty; prices compress toward 100¢ slower than efficient.

**Kill measurement:** After 12-20 bps round-trip, net hit rate × $1 payout minus losses < T-bill return on capital over identical holding windows, on ≥40 resolved contracts. If net annualized return ≤4.3%, falsified.

**Data:** Polymarket Gamma API (free, point-in-time via CLOB price history with timestamps). Historical resolution timestamps from event calendars.

**Test: Polymarket "Will [candidate] win [state]?" vs. state-level polling averages, sampled at 2pm ET daily.**

Enter long "Yes" when market implied probability trails the state's polling-average-implied probability by ≥8 points, exit at resolution or when the gap closes. Net of 12–20 bps round-trip and the 4.3% T-bill hurdle, the strategy must clear a deflated Sharpe ≥1.0 with trial accounting.

**Kill measurement:** Net-of-cost deflated Sharpe <1.0 after accounting for all trials, or a mean net edge below zero across ≥20 resolved contracts.

**Data:** Polymarket historical binary prices (free via Gamma/CLOB API, point-in-time); state polling averages (free, 538/Silver Bullet, point-in-time archived).

**Claim (b) is most likely wrong.**

PEAD's disappearance post-2006 is frequently asserted but rests on pooled, equal-weight long/short deciles with no cost overlay. Falsifier: a single-name long/short portfolio sorting on SUE (or standardized earnings surprise), implemented with realistic execution (VWAP, 12–20 bps round trip), restricted to top-1000 liquid names, holding 60–120 days, with proper trial accounting (deflated Sharpe across sort variants), still showing net IR > 0.5 after 2006. Several practitioner implementations report exactly this: the effect compressed in magnitude but survived in large caps when traded patiently and cost-aware. The "dead" claim typically reflects publication bias and implementation sloppiness, not genuine disappearance.

**(b)** is most likely wrong. The "death since ~2006" is largely a post-2010 artifact of the mega-cap growth regime, and PEAD in single-name equities has shown intermittent revival tied to rate regimes and retail flow (e.g., 2020–21). The claim conflates a specific decade's drawdown with structural disappearance.

**Falsifying observation:** A net-of-18bps long/short PEAD portfolio (SUE deciles, skip-one-day entry, 63-day holding) on Russell 1000 names delivers a deflated Sharpe (trial-adjusted, multiple-testing accounted) above the 4.3% T-bill over a post-2015 sample, robust across 2016–2019 and 2022–2024 subperiods. That would show the premium persists once mega-cap crowding and zero-commission noise are controlled.

**(b) is most likely wrong for crypto.**

Post-earnings drift "death" is an equity-market regularity tied to disclosure events and analyst coverage. Crypto has no earnings calendar, no consensus estimates, and no mandated disclosure cycle — so the finding doesn't transfer as a structural prior. The falsifiable observation: take a large-cap crypto asset with a scheduled, information-dense event (e.g., major protocol upgrade activation, spot-ETF flow disclosure, or a dominant exchange's quarterly proof-of-reserves). Measure forward returns over 5/20/60 days net of a 16 bps round trip. If the post-event drift is statistically indistinguishable from zero across a deflated-Sharpe trial accounting (and the T-bill alternative), claim (b) holds for crypto; if a persistent, cost-surviving drift appears, (b) is falsified.

**Test**: “Benchmark‑adjusted yield curve up‑re‑versal.”  
- **Procedure**: At 10‑am on a business day, run all two‑to‑five‑year U.S. Treasury‑bond ETFs and their contemporaneous 3‑, 5‑, and 10‑year Treasuries. Compute the 3‑year‑to‑5‑year yield spread and the 5‑year‑to‑10‑year yield spread.  
- **Kill Criterion**: If the ratio  
\[
\frac{\text{3‑yr‑5‑yr spread}}{\text{5‑yr‑10‑yr spread}}
\]
falls below 0.25 **exactly** on the day the portfolio’s deflated Sharpe turns zero, the test fails.  
- **Data Needed**: Daily mid‑price yields (T‑Bill: 4.3 %); Treasury futures/ETFs; free from Bloomberg Free/​Yahoo Finance.  
- **Cost Level**: 12–20 bps round‑trip on liquid 3‑ to 10‑yr Treasuries.  

If the spread‑ratio ever dips below 0.25 on a Sharpe‑zero day, the bond gamble is statistically invalidated.
